items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel about starting a new school.

Mei stood at the classroom door clutching a timetable she had folded so many times it was soft as cloth.
Twenty-eight faces turned. Someone laughed – not at her, probably, but her cheeks burned anyway.
"There's a seat here," said a girl with silver braces and paint on her fingers. She shoved a pile of comics aside. "I'm Zara. Do you like drawing? Please say yes. Nobody here likes drawing."
Mei, who had filled three sketchbooks on the plane from Shanghai, almost smiled.
"Yes," she said. It was the first word she had spoken all day.

Analyse how the writer uses sentence length and structure in this extract, with reference to "Twenty-eight faces turned.".
items.answer: Short sentence: "Twenty-eight faces turned." – the brief sentence captures the sudden, overwhelming attention Mei feels.
items.markingKey: Short sentence: "Twenty-eight faces turned." – the brief sentence captures the sudden, overwhelming attention Mei feels. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a suspense story.

The attic door had been locked for as long as Leila could remember. 'Nothing up there but dust,' Gran always said.
So why, tonight, was there a light under it?
Leila climbed the stairs. Each step creaked. Each creak sounded like a warning.
She reached for the handle. It was warm.
Behind the door, something was humming – a tune she knew. The tune her mother used to sing.
Her mother had been gone for six years.

Explain how sentence types help to create the effect of the extract, using "Her mother had been gone for six years." as one example.
items.answer: Cliffhanger: "Her mother had been gone for six years." – the final revelation shocks the reader and leaves the mystery unresolved.
items.markingKey: Cliffhanger: "Her mother had been gone for six years." – the final revelation shocks the reader and leaves the mystery unresolved. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Short sentences are a sign of weak writing."
items.answer: Short sentences are weak only when overused or accidental; used deliberately, they are a powerful stylistic tool.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: too many short sentences can feel choppy; complex ideas need complex sentences. Arguments against: short sentences create tension and emphasis; skilled writers use them deliberately. Supported judgement: Short sentences are weak only when overused or accidental; used deliberately, they are a powerful stylistic tool.

items.answer: Punctuation shows where ideas begin and end and how they relate, preventing misreading (e.g. "Let's eat, Grandma" vs "Let's eat Grandma").

items.stem:
Read the following interview from a teen magazine with a young chef in Lima.

At 16, Valentina Rojas runs a weekend food stall in Lima that sells out in two hours. We asked her how.
Q: Where did you learn to cook?
A: My abuela's kitchen. She never measured anything. She'd say, 'Cook until it smells like home.'
Q: What's the hardest part?
A: Waking up at 4 a.m. to buy fish. And being taken seriously. People ask where my parents are.
Q: Advice for other teens?
A: Start small. Burn things. Try again.

Describe the register of this text and explain why it suits its audience.
items.answer: The tone is lively and inspiring: Valentina's direct, humorous answers give energy and encouragement.
items.markingKey: The tone is lively and inspiring: Valentina's direct, humorous answers give energy and encouragement. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). items.stem: Identify three features that make this sentence informal and rewrite it formally: "Hiya! Can't make the meeting cos I've got footy, sorry!!"
items.answer: Features: greeting "Hiya", contraction "Can't", abbreviation "cos", slang "footy", double exclamation marks. Formal: "I am sorry, but I am unable to attend the meeting because I have football practice."
items.markingKey: Features: greeting "Hiya", contraction "Can't", abbreviation "cos", slang "footy", double exclamation marks. Formal: "I am sorry, but I am unable to attend the meeting because I have football practice."

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Texting and social media are damaging young people's ability to write formally."
items.answer: Most young people can switch registers when taught to; the key is awareness of audience and purpose rather than avoiding informal writing.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: abbreviations creep into school work; less practice of long formal writing. Arguments against: young people switch registers skilfully (code-switching); digital writing builds fluency and creativity. Supported judgement: Most young people can switch registers when taught to; the key is awareness of audience and purpose rather than avoiding informal writing.

items.stem: Briefly explain why choosing the right register is important.
items.answer: The wrong register can confuse, offend or weaken a message: slang in a letter to a councillor seems disrespectful, while very formal language in a text to a friend sounds cold.
